result.markdown: --- title: "Smoothing" engine: julia --- Interpolation passes through the data; for measured data with noise that is not always what you want. The Julia package smooths gridded data in two ways. `fit_scattered` fits a convolution interpolant to the data with a roughness penalty whose weight is chosen by generalized cross-validation, so nothing has to be tuned, and it reports the noise level it found. A Gaussian kernel, in `convolution_smooth` and `convolution_gaussian`, averages the data with a width you choose; it is a few separable passes over the data, orders of magnitude cheaper, and the only feasible choice in many dimensions. The Python port does not include smoothing yet; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd) tracks the port. ## Smoothing with the parameter chosen for you Gridded data are points that happen to lie on a grid, so they can be handed to the scattered-data fit of the [scattered-data page](scattered.qmd) as a matrix of coordinates, one column per point. A noisy sine: ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} Random.seed!(1) # reproducible noise x = range(0, 2π, length = 400) # a uniform grid clean = sin.(x) # the signal noisy = clean .+ 0.1 .* randn(400) # the signal with noise of standard deviation 0.1 pts = reshape(collect(x), 1, :) # the knots as a 1 × n matrix of points knots, vals, info = fit_scattered(pts, noisy) # the fitted grid, with λ chosen by cross-validation fit = convolution_interpolation(knots, vals; kernel = :a4, bc = :poly) # the interpolant, with the kernel the fit used info # the smoothing parameter and the estimated noise ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (lambda = 5.311872754985093e-15, noise = 0.10521577738539029) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} xf = range(0, 2π, length = 1000) # fine points for plotting fig = Figure(size = (800, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x") scatter!(ax, x, noisy; markersize = 5, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1, label = "noisy data") lines!(ax, xf, fit.(xf); label = "fitted interpolant") # the fit, evaluated between the knots lines!(ax, xf, sin.(xf); color = :black, label = "signal") # the signal it was recovering Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | | noisy data | fitted interpolant | |:--|--:|--:| | rms error against the signal | 0.1061 | 0.0217 | The noise standard deviation estimated by the fit is 0.1052; the noise was generated with 0.1. The result is an interpolant, so derivatives and integrals of the smoothed signal come from the same object, as on the other pages. The fit's grid is as fine as the data density allows, so that nothing the points resolve is lost before the smoothing is chosen, and it warns, pointing at the `oversample` keyword, when the fitted smoothing would need a finer grid still. It solves a sparse system, so it costs more than a pass over the data, and the system grows with the dimension. The same fit on the same noise, with the signal's frequency raised, shows what the cross-validation does: the smoothing follows the signal, not a preset width. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The fit at several signal frequencies"} ks = (1, 3, 10, 30) # cycles over the interval fit_errors = map(ks) do k cleank = sin.(k .* x) # the signal at this frequency Random.seed!(1) noisyk = cleank .+ 0.1 .* randn(400) # the same noise realisation kn, vl, _ = fit_scattered(pts, noisyk) rms(convolution_interpolation(kn, vl; kernel = :a4, bc = :poly).(x) .- cleank) end; ``` ::: | cycles over the interval | 1 | 3 | 10 | 30 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | rms error of the fit | 0.0217 | 0.0239 | 0.0355 | 0.0529 | ## Gaussian smoothing The Gaussian kernel has a single parameter `B`, the width in units of the grid spacing: the weight of a neighbour $k$ spacings away is proportional to $\exp(-B k^2)$. So a larger `B` is a narrower kernel and less smoothing; a smaller `B` is a wider kernel and more smoothing. The weights are normalised to sum to one, so the mean level of the data is preserved. Around `B ≈ 0.1` the result is usually good, and the optimum is shallow, so precise tuning rarely pays. The same noisy sine, smoothed on the grid at a range of widths: ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} smoothed_01 = convolution_smooth(x, noisy, 0.1); # smoothed values on the grid, B = 0.1 ``` ::: | B | 2.0 | 1.0 | 0.5 | 0.2 | 0.1 | 0.05 | 0.02 | 0.01 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | rms error after smoothing | 0.0872 | 0.0709 | 0.0595 | 0.0483 | 0.0418 | 0.0361 | 0.0294 | 0.0264 | Too narrow a kernel leaves the noise; too wide a kernel flattens the peaks of the signal. The table shows the shallow optimum between the two — and, against the fit's table above, that the best `B` lands a little behind the fit, which was not told the width. A single width also cannot follow a signal whose frequency changes across the data, where the fit's roughness penalty can. ### In more dimensions The Gaussian smoothing is separable, one axis at a time, so it costs about the same per value in any number of dimensions: ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} Random.seed!(2) xs = range(0, 2π, length = 150) # the grid along x ys = range(0, 2π, length = 150) # the grid along y field = [cos(xi) * sin(yi) for xi in xs, yi in ys] # the signal noisy2 = field .+ 0.2 .* randn(150, 150) # with noise smoothed = convolution_smooth((xs, ys), noisy2, 0.1) # smoothed values on the grid fig = Figure(size = (800, 760)) for (pos, z, name) in ((fig[1, 1], noisy2, "noisy"), (fig[1, 2], smoothed, "smoothed, B = 0.1"), (fig[2, 1:2], field, "signal")) ax = Axis(pos; title = name, aspect = DataAspect()) heatmap!(ax, xs, ys, z; colorrange = (-1.2, 1.2)) end fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | | noisy | smoothed | |:--|--:|--:| | rms error | 0.2013 | 0.0289 | ### Evaluating between the knots `convolution_gaussian` builds the same smoothing as an interpolant, so it can be evaluated at any point, not only on the grid. Between the knots the Gaussian weights sum to slightly less than one, and the sum deviates more the narrower the kernel; up to `B = 0.34` the deviation is below $10^{-12}$, which is why `convolution_gaussian` accepts `B` up to that value only, while `convolution_smooth`, which evaluates on the knots, takes any `B`. ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} itp = convolution_gaussian(x, noisy, 0.1) # the smoothing as an interpolant itp(1.5), itp.(x[1:3]) # anywhere, or on the knots ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1.060036287602848, [0.023641958315981988, 0.0281590116155507, 0.03509202752853787]) ``` ::: ::: On the knots it agrees with `convolution_smooth`: ``` {.julia .cell-code} @printf("The largest difference on the knots is %.2e.\n", maximum(abs.(itp.(x) .- convolution_smooth(x, noisy, 0.1)))) ``` The largest difference on the knots is 4.44e-15. ## Which to use - The fit, when the result matters more than the time: it chooses the smoothing, estimates the noise, follows the signal's own scale, and returns an interpolant. Its cost grows with the grid and the dimension. - The Gaussian, when the data are large or high-dimensional, or when the width is known. It is a few microseconds per thousand values, in any number of dimensions. Both lose some accuracy near the boundaries, where the ghost values are extrapolated from noisy data; that is a property of any local method, not of the kernel. The [smoothing benchmark](../benchmarks/julia/smoothing.qmd) compares both with the alternatives, in accuracy and in time, across noise levels and signal frequencies.
